title: The harrowing of hell
hookLine: the Orthodox Easter icon: Christ breaking the gates of death and pulling Adam and Eve up by the wrists

cards: The doors are broken. In the icon, two heavy gates lie flat, and scattered around them are keys, bolts and broken locks. Christ stands on the fallen doors, dressed in white, reaching down with both hands.
On one side an old man is being pulled up out of a tomb. On the other, an old woman. Adam and Eve.
And look at the hands. He isn't holding theirs. He has them by the wrists, the way you'd pull someone out of deep water.
This is the icon Orthodox Christians set out for Easter. Its story belongs to the Saturday in between. Today, the harrowing of hell.

teach.h: THE SATURDAY THE GOSPELS LEAVE QUIET.
teach.b: Holy Saturday is the day the Gospels leave almost silent. The body is in the tomb. Luke says the women who had followed Jesus rested on the sabbath, as the law asked.
That's nearly all. So where was he? Christians answered from a few lines.
One is First Peter, about Christ put to death in the flesh, in the King James: "By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison."

The old creed, in the Book of Common Prayer, runs: "He descended into hell; The third day he rose again from the dead." In the icon, hell means the place of the dead, where those who died before him wait.
And a psalm gives the picture of the doors: "For he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder." Put together, it's a rescue story.
In that picture death is a prison, and on the Saturday the one who died goes in, breaks the gates from the inside, and starts pulling people out, beginning with the first two in the human story.

teach.h: HE HOLDS THEM BY THE WRISTS.
teach.b: That's why the wrists matter. Adam and Eve don't climb out by hanging on tight. They're held.
Orthodox Christians and Catholics both keep this teaching, and Anglicans and Lutherans who use the Apostles' Creed say its line.
Some Protestant readers take First Peter in other ways, and some churches say the creed as he descended to the dead. The icon doesn't settle those debates. It just shows the hands.

how: Orthodox churches display the icon of the resurrection, which shows Christ breaking the gates of death and raising Adam and Eve, at Easter; Western churches that use the Apostles' Creed say its line about the descent, and some remember it on Holy Saturday.

games.q: the icon and its texts — tap the pairs.
p: preached unto the spirits in prison

s: in the icon, Adam and Eve climb out by holding on tight
he grips them by the wrists. the rescue doesn't depend on their grip.
the Gospels describe in detail what Jesus did on Holy Saturday
they're nearly silent: the body lies in the tomb, and the women rest on the sabbath.
the old creed says "he descended into hell"
in the Book of Common Prayer: "He descended into hell; The third day he rose again from the dead."

games.q: you're Adam, in the dark place of the dead. the gates crash down and a hand reaches toward you. what happens?
o: you have to climb out on your own.
he takes you by the wrist and pulls you out.
you're told to wait a little longer.
games.why: in the icon, Christ has Adam and Eve by the wrists. they're held, not hanging on.

practice: Find an image of the icon, often called the Anastasis, or hold the picture from a minute ago in mind.
Look first at the broken doors underfoot, then at the hands closed around the wrists, then at Adam and Eve, old and tired and being lifted, and let your eye rest where it wants.
If you pray, let the looking be prayer; if not, simply stay with the image.

wordCard.voice: Holy Saturday. The day Christ, Christians teach, went down to the dead, broke the gates, and brought them out, with Adam and Eve first.

orig.note: Greek: resurrection — the name given to this Easter icon.
